text: Nitro-aromatic scaffolds often correlate with hepatotoxicity via reactive metabolites. The nitro group undergoes nitroreduction to form reactive nitroso and hydroxylamine intermediates.
Drugs with high lipophilicity (LogP > 4) and molecular weight > 400 Da show increased risk of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). Monitor ALT/AST levels.
Acetaminophen-like structures with para-aminophenol can cause hepatotoxicity through NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) formation when glutathione is depleted.
hERG channel blockers with basic nitrogen and aromatic rings may cause QT prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias. Common in antihistamines, antipsychotics, and antibiotics.
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with aortic aneurysm and dissection risk. The mechanism involves collagen degradation via MMP activation.
Lipophilic molecules with TPSA < 50 Å² frequently cross the BBB and may trigger CNS side effects including sedation, dizziness, and seizures.
Anticholinergic drugs can cause cognitive impairment, confusion, and delirium, especially in elderly. Common structural features include tertiary amines and aromatic rings.
Serotonin syndrome risk increases with drugs containing tryptamine scaffolds or MAO inhibitors. Symptoms include hyperthermia, agitation, and tremor.
Sulfonamide motifs can induce hypersensitivity reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Cross-reactivity may occur between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides.
Beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins) are common causes of drug allergy. The beta-lactam ring can act as a hapten after binding to proteins.
Drugs with aromatic amine groups can be metabolized to reactive nitroso compounds, leading to idiosyncratic drug reactions and autoimmune-like symptoms.
Aminoglycoside antibiotics accumulate in renal proximal tubules, causing nephrotoxicity. Risk factors include prolonged use, dehydration, and concurrent nephrotoxic drugs.
NSAIDs can cause acute kidney injury by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, leading to reduced renal blood flow. Risk is higher in patients with pre-existing renal impairment.
NSAIDs cause GI ulceration by inhibiting COX-1-mediated prostaglandin synthesis. Risk is dose-dependent and increased with concurrent corticosteroid use.
Antibiotics can disrupt gut microbiome, leading to Clostridium difficile infection and diarrhea. Broad-spectrum antibiotics carry higher risk.
Drugs with quinone or hydroquinone structures can cause methemoglobinemia by oxidizing hemoglobin. Symptoms include cyanosis and dyspnea.
Chloramphenicol and other drugs with nitrobenzene groups can cause aplastic anemia through bone marrow suppression. This is an idiosyncratic reaction.
Photosensitizing drugs (fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, NSAIDs) can cause phototoxic reactions. Advise patients to avoid sun exposure during treatment.
Drugs causing Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) often contain aromatic amines or sulfonamides. HLA-B*5801 is a genetic risk factor for allopurinol-induced SJS.
Atypical antipsychotics can cause metabolic syndrome including weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia. Mechanism involves 5-HT2C and H1 receptor antagonism.
Thiazide diuretics can cause hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hyperuricemia. Monitor electrolytes and uric acid levels during therapy.
Lipinski's Rule of Five: MW ≤ 500, LogP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10. Violations correlate with poor oral bioavailability and increased toxicity risk.
Veber's rules: Rotatable bonds ≤ 10 and TPSA ≤ 140 Å² for good oral bioavailability. High flexibility reduces membrane permeability.
Reactive metabolites from CYP450 metabolism can form protein adducts, leading to idiosyncratic toxicity. Common bioactivation pathways include epoxidation, quinone formation, and N-oxidation.
Michael acceptors (α,β-unsaturated carbonyls) are electrophilic and can form covalent bonds with proteins, leading to toxicity. Common in acrylamide-containing drugs.
Epoxides are highly reactive electrophiles that can alkylate DNA and proteins. They are often formed as metabolites of aromatic compounds.
Aldehydes can form Schiff bases with lysine residues, leading to protein modification. Aldehyde-containing drugs may cause tissue irritation and toxicity.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) can be metabolized to diol-epoxides, which are potent mutagens and carcinogens.
Drug-drug interactions often occur at CYP3A4, CYP2D6, and CYP2C9 enzymes. Inhibitors can increase plasma levels of co-administered drugs, enhancing toxicity.
P-glycoprotein (P-gp) substrates may have reduced CNS penetration but increased GI toxicity. P-gp inhibitors can alter drug distribution and efficacy.
Kinase inhibitors often cause skin rash and diarrhea due to EGFR inhibition in epithelial tissues. Hepatotoxicity may occur with multi-kinase inhibitors.
HDAC inhibitors can cause thrombocytopenia and fatigue. Cardiac effects including QT prolongation have been reported.
